Open Policy Analysis for:

California Proposition 40, Reconciliation of the Two Analyses

Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, would tax Californians worth $1 billion or more once, at 5% of their net worth, paid over five years. The BSZ analysis (Boll, Saez and Zucman, NBER, August 2026) finds that it raises money for the state. The JR analysis (Jaros and Rauh, NBER, September 2026) finds that it leaves the state $39.0B poorer, because billionaires who leave stop paying California income tax for ever. This page puts both on one definition and shows which assumptions make the difference. It follows the Open Policy Analysis (OPA) framework.

BSZ main estimate1 $106.8B Net total: the wealth tax plus the income tax it changes, over 5 years, in today's dollars
JR main estimate1 −$39.0B Net present value: the wealth tax minus the income tax lost for ever, in today's dollars, averaged over the authors' model runs (Jaros and Rauh, September 2026)

Today's dollars (present value): what money received or lost in future years is worth now.

What separates the two numbers

$106.8BBSZ estimate −$29.9BBillionaires already departed −$39.4BChance the tax does not survive litigation −$81.3BLost income tax +$4.9BThe other three steps together ≈−$39.0BJR estimate

Move the explorer's BSZ panel to the JR values one group at a time, from left to right: the departed wealth, the chance the tax survives in court, the four inputs of the lost income tax, then the other three. Each term is what its group changes. The report gives all nine steps.

How AI was used in this exercise, and what has been verified #

who did what, and what a person has checked

This work was a collaboration between the author and Claude Code (Opus and Sonnet models) across many sessions, not an AI working alone. The table records who led the work on each public object of the comparison, using the CRediT contributor roles. The author gave these answers in a questionnaire on 2026-10-15, all 14 roles and the verification question for each object; they were not inferred from commit history. Funding does not apply. Resources (computing and analysis tools) are not in the table. Claude led them for the explorer and this page, and they do not apply to the other objects. Human verification: not reviewed lightly reviewed reviewed

Human verification uses three levels: not reviewed, lightly reviewed (checked, but the author cannot yet explain it clearly) and reviewed (the author can explain it to others). The automated test suites are mechanical checks, not an outside review. No other person has verified this work, and the original authors have not reviewed it.

This OPA and the Hoopes comparison #

the one published comparison, and what this OPA adds

Jeffrey Hoopes (SSRN 6428578, 2026) is the one published comparison of the two estimates. It compares earlier versions: the February 2026 GGSS expert report (Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske), on which the BSZ analysis builds, and the March 2026 JR analysis. Its Figure 2 prints no values and comes with no code or data, so its steps cannot be recomputed. This OPA uses the latest versions, publishes the code, and bridges the two estimates step by step. The report sets his bars beside this bridge, difference by difference.

"Guesswork on data" is a judgement applied to observed facts. "Derived" is a value computed from the analysis's own inputs: the JR discount rate is the one rate worth the same as the authors' random draw of it.

1 Each analysis's own main estimate. The BSZ number is this OPA's net total over 5 years at 3%: the $103.8B wealth tax (Table 5 row 1), plus income tax from asset sales, minus income tax lost to leavers. BSZ's own headline is the wealth tax alone. The JR number is the authors' mean net present value in perpetuity. The paper prints −$38.9B, the average of one seeded run of 100,000 draws. The exact average of the same formula is −$38.98B, used throughout this page (report, Step 6 of the JR analysis's report). The report gives the details.
